questions.stem: FSH is released from the pituitary gland at the start of the menstrual cycle. What are the two main effects of FSH?

options.text: Causes the uterus lining to break down and inhibits oestrogen production
Stimulates the maturation of a follicle in the ovary and promotes oestrogen production by the ovary
Triggers ovulation and causes the corpus luteum to form
Maintains the uterus lining and prevents menstruation

questions.explanation: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) stimulates a follicle to develop in the ovary, and the developing follicle produces oestrogen. These are the key early events in the menstrual cycle that prepare the body for potential ovulation and pregnancy.

questions.stem: Around day 14 of the menstrual cycle, a surge of LH occurs. What does this LH surge trigger?

options.text: The breakdown of the uterus lining (menstruation)
The start of follicle development in the ovary
Ovulation — the release of a mature egg from the ovary
The production of FSH by the pituitary gland

questions.explanation: The surge in LH (luteinising hormone) around day 14 triggers ovulation — the release of a mature egg from the ovary. After ovulation, LH also stimulates the empty follicle to develop into the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone.

questions.stem: Progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum after ovulation. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels drop. What is the consequence of this drop?

options.text: A new egg is immediately released from the ovary
The thick uterus lining can no longer be maintained and breaks down, causing menstruation
FSH production is permanently stopped
The corpus luteum grows larger and produces more oestrogen

questions.explanation: Progesterone maintains the thick, blood-rich uterus lining needed for embryo implantation. When the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone levels fall, the lining cannot be maintained and is shed — this is menstruation, marking the start of a new cycle.

questions.stem: Oestrogen has a dual role in the menstrual cycle. At low levels it inhibits LH release, but at high levels it stimulates a surge of LH. What type of feedback does the LH surge represent?

options.text: Negative feedback — oestrogen reduces LH to maintain balance
Positive feedback — rising oestrogen stimulates an LH surge, which triggers ovulation
No feedback — LH release is random and uncontrolled
Negative feedback — LH inhibits oestrogen production

questions.explanation: This is an example of positive feedback: the rising oestrogen levels from the developing follicle stimulate (rather than inhibit) a large release of LH from the pituitary. This LH surge triggers ovulation. Positive feedback amplifies the change rather than counteracting it.

questions.stem: A couple is trying to conceive. They know that the woman's cycle is 28 days long. On which days is she most likely to be fertile, and why?

options.text: Days 1-5, when menstruation occurs and the uterus lining is shedding
Days 12-16, around ovulation when a mature egg has been released and is available for fertilisation
Days 22-28, when progesterone levels are highest
She is equally fertile on every day of the cycle

questions.explanation: Ovulation typically occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle. The egg survives for about 24 hours after release, and sperm can survive for up to 5 days in the female reproductive tract. Therefore, the fertile window is approximately days 12-16.
